content.title: Reducing teenage pregnancies in Uganda
content.summary: SONAM Uganda research provides insight into reproductive health services for teen mums

media.caption: Harriet Nayiga (standing) interacts with teenagers in 2019

content.text: When AKU-SONAM alumna, Harriet Nayiga started MILCOT in 2017, she was excited but also knew that it would involve commitment and a lot of hard work.

Midwife-led Community Transformation (MILCOT) was established as an indigenous organization as a result of witnessing teenagers in the poorest and most marginalised areas become pregnant. MILCOT, therefore, situated itself in one of the poorest areas of Kampala: Nansana Municipality in Wakiso District, north-west of Kampala City.

There are very few midwives outside hospital settings who work with the youth in communities to provide sexual and reproductive health information to adolescents and young adults. This leaves many young people vulnerable to myths and misconceptions from peers, traditional birth attendants and herbalists. The organization is supported by a committed team of volunteer midwives, programme officers, social workers and a clinical psychologist. It provides the necessary sexual reproductive health information to young people to reduce teenage pregnancies and the deaths of mothers and babies.
The worrying trend of maternal and reproductive health in Uganda
In Uganda, the teenage birth rate stands at 140 per 1,000 adolescent girls. The unmet need for contraception stands at 28 per cent and is higher among teenagers.

Despite great strides made by the country, the maternal mortality rate still stands at 336 deaths per 100,000 live births and is among the highest on the continent and in the world. As a result, Uganda's Minister of Health, Dr Jane Ruth Aceng called on stakeholders to devise strategies to bring the rates down.

There is a critical shortage of nurses and midwives globally. In Uganda, it is estimated that 74% of births are performed by a skilled birth attendant. The present ratio of nurses and midwives per 1,000 population falls far short of the minimum rate recommended by the World Health Organization as documented in
The State of the World's Midwifery Report
Teenagers at risk in Wakiso district

Wakiso district plays home to a community with high poverty levels, with most people living in slums, and high levels of prostitution. The Uganda Demographic Health Survey of 2016 reported that in Wakiso district, 6 per cent of girls aged 12 to 17 had already given birth and 6.5 per cent of the girls aged 12 to 17 years had been in a marriage union.

MILCOT focuses on four programme areas: promoting personal health and survival initiatives; building the capacity of midwives and nurses through confidence training and leadership and knowledge; upskilling initiatives and social enterprise programmes.
It is believed that these areas will strengthen initiatives and build the capacity of midwives and nurses in Uganda to focus on prevention.

MILCOT assessed five surrounding villages in Nansana Municipality before the start of the project. From a total of 120 respondents, nearly half were not living with their biological parents but lived in other places such as brothels or homes managed by a brothel owner. Thirty-two per cent were reported to be living with community members. This highlights the high exposure to risky behaviour for adolescents and young adults in Nansana. A few of the adolescents had various forms of disability and had never received any information relating to sexual and reproductive health rights.

To date, MILCOT has provided 420 adolescents and young adults with information and counselling services, particularly on sexual reproductive health rights, counselled and educated 15 mothers with psychotherapy to deal with post-natal stress, post-miscarriage stress and depression associated with domestic violence and severe poverty. Additionally, it has trained 200 adolescents and young adults in life skills (including self-reliance, interpersonal skills and effective decision-making) and established a drop-in centre to respond to day-to-day reproductive health challenges of adolescents and young adults who call on MILCOT after becoming aware of health community outreaches.

In the future, MILCOT hopes to build the resilience of midwives and nurses in effective and efficient preventive and responsive service delivery and improve links with responsive reproductive health and rights services within the Nansana municipality.
